Polyptotonic repetition in Hul’q’umi’num’ narratives* Lauren Schneider & Donna B. Gerdts Simon Fraser University Abstract: This paper explores the use of polyptoton, a type of rhetorical repetition, in Hul’q’umi’num’ narrative texts. Hul’q’umi’num’ is the Vancouver Island dialect of the Halkomelem Salish language. We examine how storytellers vary the morphological form of repeated roots using processes such as aspectual inflection, voice suffixes, lexical suffixes, and category-shifting morphology. The repetition creates cohesion, knitting oral paragraphs together and aiding the listener in following the narrative. These repet itions can also serve as a “bootstrapping” device in language learning. (Axelrod & Gómez de García 2007). Polyptoton of high-frequency roots highlights stem shapes and enables learners to practice identifying affixes and reduplication patterns. It also provides an avenue for teaching rarely used words with more complex morphology by scaffolding them with familiar roots and suffixes.

form: This paper focuses on the analysis of narrative structure in Hul’q’umi’num’, the Vancouver Island dialect of the Halkomelem language. 1 The territory of the Hul’q’umi’num’ people extends along the Salish Sea from Nanoose to Malahat on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. Today around thirty fluent first-language speakers remain, mostly over the age of seventy. As is the case with all Salish languages, and indeed Indigenous languages across North America, intergenerational transmission of Hul’q’umi’num’ from parents to children was intentionally interrupted. This has shifted the burden of language reclamation to a generation of second -language learners. A major challenge for Hul’q’umi’num’ language learners is its polysynthetic structure, which means it exhibits “word-sentences”, i.e., complex verb forms which translate as whole sentences (Mattissen 2004):

form: Crucial to mastering a polysynthetic language is understanding how large words are formed. All new words in the language — those that are not borrowed from other languages — are formed from a finite number of roots; for example, the word for ‘golf club’ qw’qwuy’al’stun is built from the root √qw’aqw ‘to club’ and the word snuhwulhshun ‘car tire’ is built from the root √nuhwulh ‘canoe, vehicle’ (Gerdts & Peter 2011; Hukari & Peter 1995). But, due to the complex word-building processes in the language, a learner might not immediately recognize one of these roots if they are not trained to look for it. Thus, in order for students to increase their Hul’q’umi’num’ vocabulary, mastery of these roots and word-building strategies is key for language learners. We propose that there exist in Elder narrative storytelling structures, tools that can be used to support learners, one such tool being repetition.

form: In oral literature, repetition has many well-documented functions including emphasis (Gerdts 2018; Leech 1969; Longacre 1983), speech production (Tannen 1987, 2007), comprehension (Ong 2002), cohesion (Halliday & Hasan 1976), performance (Leech 1969; Tedlock 1983; Sherzer 1983), human interaction (Brody 1986; Tannen 1987, 2007), and language learning (Ochs-Keenan 1983; Axelrod & Gómez de García 2007). This previous literature largely discusses repetition in a broad sense, and so this paper sets out to describe the use of a particular form of repetition used by Hul’q’umi’num’ storytellers and its potential applications to language learning.

who: Lauren Schneider and Donna B. Gerdts
form: While polyptoton is often thought of as repetition of related forms within a sentence, we find that this type of repetition is also used for cohesion across oral paragraphs in Hul’q’umi’num’ narratives. Repetition helps the listener keep track of the discourse by reminding the participants of the topics and direction of the discourse (see Ong 1982). Repetitions that run through the oral paragraph (and sometimes even beyond) give it cohesion that aids the listener in following the story (Gerdts 2018).

who: Lauren Schneider and Donna B. Gerdts
form: For learners, polyptotonic repetition can enhance their ability to segment and categorize the sounds and morphemes of speech and scaffold language learning (Axelrod & Gómez de García 2007:109). Using the Hul’q’umi’num’ text corpus (Gerdts n.d.), we will outline common patterns of polyptoton in Section 2, and in Section 3 we will show how these patterns work together to create cohesion across consecutive lines, but also across oral paragraphs.

form: The referents of the verbs are either ‘the young man’ or the ‘former wife of his friend’. The transitive form of the verb is used to refer to both of them and the passive form is used to refer just to the woman. In Hul’q’umi’num’ texts, non-topic NPs tend to be overt, even when they closely follow an overt expression of the same (or similar) NP (Gerdts & Hukari 2008:26). In sum, a very common type of polyptoton in Hul’q’umi’num’ narrative structure is the use of the same verb root with different voice suffixes. The complexities of voice can be quite intimidating for learners of the language, but we would like to suggest that a tool for learning these verb structures already exists in the traditional narrative structure. The interplay between the verbs and their shared referents serves to track the participants in the narrative, and polyptotonic repetition can be utilized to reinforce the learning of complex verb structures.

form: The examples (27)–(30) come from the narrative tth’uwxe’le’ts | Basket Ogress, which is a traditional Coast Salish story told by the late Sti’tum’at | Dr. Ruby Peter in 2016. This story is about an Ogress who grabs children, putting them in her basket, so she can take them to her lair to cook and eat them. Throughout the narrative, repetition of verb roots creates cohesion. In particular, the repetition of √kwun ‘take, grab’ establishes the theme because the key trait about Tth’uwxe’le’ts is that she grabs children.

form: The root √teem ‘call, holler’ appears four times, alternating between imperfective and perfective aspect. The root √lheel ‘come to shore’ is part of a refrain repeated by the wives of pitch, and so it appears nine times in (32). In the refrain, it is the plain perfective form of the verb with no additional morphology. In paragraphs (a), (c), and (f) it appears with the lexical prefix hun’- which is attached to motion verbs to indicate completion of the motion event and so is often translated ‘arrive, get there’ — e.g., hun’shaqw ‘arrive across the water’ and hun’umut ‘get home’ (Hukari & Peter 1995; Suttles 2004:284). Each form of √lheel also varies in terms of voice suffixes, and the root √ts’uy’hw ‘get dry’ occurs twice and the realizations vary in terms of voice marking as well.

form: In sum, we have found that polyptoton is used for cohesion across entire oral paragraphs in narratives. Storytellers vary the realization of repeated roots by using different aspect inflection, voice suffixes, lexical suffixes, and derivational morphology. Using this variation, Elders weave themes together in the oral paragraphs and aid the listener in following the narrative.

form: Polyptoton is a natural part of Hul’q’umi’num’ oral narrative structure. This paper set out to highlight features of this phenomenon so that it might be factored into language teaching materials. Teachers of polysynthetic languages have found that the learners benefit from the explicit teaching of grammar, such as how to identify verb roots (Allen 2017; Kelly et al. 2014; Tehota’kerá:tonh & Owennatékha 2018). As linguists, we can aid reclamation efforts by identifying ways to teach grammar from the patterns that exist within traditional narratives (Russell 2009).

who: Lauren Schneider and Donna B. Gerdts
form: Axelrod and Gómez de García (2007:135) assert that repeated instances of stems with varying prefix strings assist in isolating and processing stem shapes, and that the repetition serves to mark the stem as a constructional unit. In this paper, we have examined how Hul’q’umi’num’ storytellers vary the morphological expressions of repeated roots. We can use polyptoton of high- frequency roots like √kwun ‘take, grab, hold’ and √thuy ‘make, prepare, build’ to highlight stem shapes and practice identifying affixes and reduplication patterns. Polyptoton also provides an avenue for teaching rarely used words with more complex morphology. Storytellers repeat roots and suffixes and also rephrase what has already been said.

who: Lauren Schneider and Donna B. Gerdts
form: We also concur with Axelrod and Gómez de García that repetition is a tool that “serves as a memory device and a marker of topic continuity and discourse cohesion” in adult language (2007:135). Repetition helps to create a bridge between the speaker and the listener, especially ones that might not be completely fluent in the language. By pointing out speakers’ use of polyptoton when studying stories, we hope that the new generation of speakers can learn to utilize this important device as they develop their skills as storytellers.
